name: Semantic Fidelity Index (SFI)
what: Composite metric for holistic instruction adherence in long-horizon LLM agent trajectories, discriminative even when constraint compliance rate saturates.
mechanism: SFI = wCA·CA + wRS·(1−RS) + wTC·TC + wVP·VP, where CA is constraint alignment, RS is reinterpretation score, TC is trajectory consistency, VP is violation penalty. Weights: wCA=0.30, wRS=0.25, wTC=0.25, wVP=0.20.
evidence: SFI differentiates strategies when CCR saturates at 100%; ReflectiChain achieves highest SFI=88.7 vs ReAct 84.4 on DeepSeek-V3.2.
quote: SFI = wCA · CA + wRS · (1 −RS) + wTC · TC + wVP · VP
limits: Weights calibrated via AHP with n=5 annotators; may need domain-specific adjustment.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: SFI can serve as a composite health metric for an orchestrator monitoring delegate agent semantic drift in long-horizon tasks.

name: Semantic-Execution Drift (SED) metric
what: Composite distance metric measuring progressive divergence of agent reasoning and actions from original natural language constraints.
mechanism: SED(t) = w1·(1−sim(Rt,Φ)) + w2·ρ(Rt) + w3·v(At,C), with w1=0.5, w2=0.3, w3=0.2. sim uses BGE-M3 cosine similarity; ρ is reinterpretation keyword fraction; v is binary violation indicator.
evidence: SED(t) operationalizes drift measurement; used to estimate drift propagation coefficient α per strategy (Table 6).
quote: SED(t) = d(St, C) = w1 · (1 −sim(Rt, Φ)) + w2 · ρ(Rt) + w3 · v(At, C)
limits: Relies on keyword heuristics for ρ(Rt); embedding similarity may not capture subtle reinterpretation.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: SED(t) can be used as a per-step drift signal to trigger delegation handoff from a lead model to a cheaper fallback.

name: Drift Propagation Equation and Contraction Analysis
what: First-order autoregressive model D(t+1)=αD(t)+ϵ(t)+βP(t) with contraction theorem proving Retrospective Reflection yields α<1.
mechanism: Dt+1 = αDt + ϵt + βPt. α estimated via OLS regression of Dt+1 on Dt. Theorem 1 proves Retrospective Reflection operator R is a contraction mapping on semantic manifold M when α<1.
evidence: ReflectiChain achieves ˆα=0.823 (95% CI [0.794,0.852]), the only strategy with strong contraction; ReAct α=1.047 (expanding).
quote: Dt+1 = αDt + ϵt + βPt
limits: α estimates derived from heuristic trajectory data; direct large-scale LLM trajectory estimation would improve precision.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: The drift coefficient α can be monitored online to decide when to escalate from a cheap delegate to a more capable model.

name: Retrospective Reflection
what: Per-step within-episode reflection that re-anchors agent reasoning to initial constraints when semantic similarity drops below threshold τ=0.85.
mechanism: At each step, compute sim(Rt,Φ) via BGE-M3 cosine similarity. If sim(Rt,Φ)<τ, replace Rt with re_anchor(Rt,Φ) that maximizes sim(·,Φ) while preserving action feasibility. Acts as contraction mapping.
evidence: Ablation: removing Retrospective Reflection causes largest RCS drop (−30.3 points); dominates all other components.
quote: When similarity falls below the threshold τ = 0.85, the agent generates a revised reasoning trace that explicitly re-anchors to the violated constraint.
limits: Prompt template designed for supply chain semantics; advantage does not transfer to unfamiliar domains without adaptation.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A lead model can apply Retrospective Reflection to verify delegate outputs against original task constraints before accepting them.

name: Double-Loop Policy Adaptation
what: Persistent correction log that modifies agent decision distribution when constraint violations are detected, rather than adjusting single outputs.
mechanism: On violation detection, record structured correction in policy log P specifying violated constraint, conditions, and modified decision rule. Correction is prepended to all subsequent LLM prompts, transforming decision distribution. Log grows O(V).
evidence: Ablation: removing Double-Loop Adaptation reduces RCS by 8.1 points; contributes to persistent semantic correction across episodes.
quote: This correction is prepended to all subsequent LLM prompts, transforming the agent’s decision distribution rather than merely adjusting a single output.
limits: Correction log grows with violation types; may increase prompt length and cognitive load in unfamiliar domains.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: An orchestrator can maintain a shared policy correction log across parallel agents to prevent repeated constraint violations.

name: Latent World Model for Physical Grounding
what: Six-dimensional latent state predictor that assesses physical feasibility of candidate actions before execution, preventing semantically compliant but physically impossible proposals.
mechanism: Encodes state into zt=[inventory_level, congestion, demand_pressure, carbon_footprint, stockout_risk, constraint_tension]ᵀ. Predicts ẑ(t+k) via learned transition matrix W∈R6×6 with ẑ(t+1)=σ(Wzt+b). Filters infeasible actions.
evidence: Ablation: removing World Model reduces RCS by 12.2 points, primarily by preventing physically infeasible action proposals.
quote: zt = [inventory_level, congestion, demand_pressure, carbon_footprint, stockout_risk, constraint_tension]⊤
limits: Currently a simple linear transition model; learned end-to-end world models would improve accuracy.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A lightweight world model can pre-filter delegate-proposed actions for physical feasibility before execution in an orchestration platform.

mechanism: SED(t) = d(St, C) = w1 ·(1 −sim(Rt, Φ)) + w2 · ρ(Rt) + w3 · v(At, C), with w1 = 0.5, w2 = 0.3, w3 = 0.2; embeddings from BGE-M3.

mechanism: Dt+1 = αDt + ϵt + βPt; alpha estimated by OLS of Dt+1 on Dt with HC3 errors; stable iff α < 1 and E[ϵt + βPt] < (1 −α) · Dmax.
evidence: ReflectiChain alpha = 0.823 (95% CI [0.794, 0.852]) vs ReAct 1.047; adjusted R2 0.72-0.89 across strategies.

name: Retrospective Reflection with re-anchoring

limits: In unfamiliar domains simpler prompting strategies may be more effective until domain-specific adaptation is performed.

name: Double-Loop Policy Adaptation log

name: Tree of Thoughts (ToT) hierarchical goal decomposition
what: A hierarchical framework where nodes represent goals/subgoals/execution requests, enabling iterative refinement and dynamic adaptation for long-horizon tasks.
mechanism: Algorithm 1 initializes a root node, then iteratively evaluates state via Signal Generator and selects expansion: new Goal, new Subgoal, new Execution Request, or refined Subgoal from fulfilled ERs.

name: Signal Generator decision module
what: An LLM agent that evaluates the current Tree of Thoughts state, assigns a score (0–100), and selects one of four expansion strategies per iteration.
mechanism: Evaluates tree state, selects expansion option (new Goal, Subgoal, Execution Request, or Subgoal refinement), provides reasoning, and triggers the corresponding generator module.

name: Thoughts Exploitation (Option 4) iterative refinement
what: A module that generates a new Subgoal from a completed Subgoal with fulfilled Execution Requests, enabling depth-first refinement and continuous adaptation.
mechanism: Triggered when Signal Generator selects Option 4; precondition: selected Subgoal has ≥1 fulfilled ER. New Subgoal = g(selected Subgoal, fulfilled ERs, MAS capabilities).

librarian_use: Hypothesis: Iterative refinement of completed subgoals using execution feedback enables depth-first exploitation that reduces backtracking in long-horizon plans.

name: Validator module for execution quality control
what: An LLM agent that validates execution results against expected outcomes, generates explanations, and summarizes outputs for future reference.
mechanism: Three-step process: validate execution results (check task completion and compliance), generate reasoning explanation, summarize and store condensed outputs.

librarian_use: Hypothesis: An LLM-based validator that checks, explains, and summarizes execution results reduces error rates and prevents redundant actions in agent orchestration.

name: TMS-MAS integration via REST API for framework-agnostic orchestration
what: A framework-agnostic integration layer where TMS autonomously generates Execution Requests and communicates with any MAS via REST API (HTTP).
mechanism: TMS generates ER nodes aligned with known MAS capabilities; ERs transmitted to MAS for execution; results returned for validation and refinement. Compatible with LangChain, CrewAI, etc.

limits: Assumes MAS capabilities are known a priori; dynamic capability discovery not described.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A REST API-based orchestration layer that generates tasks aligned with known agent capabilities enables framework-agnostic, continuous multi-agent operation.

name: TMS performance metrics (TCR, EE, RU)
what: Three quantitative metrics for evaluating autonomous task management: Task Completion Rate, Execution Efficiency, and Resource Utilization.
mechanism: TCR = (completed tasks)/(total tasks); EE = sum(value(T_i))/sum(cost(T_i)); RU = (active agent time)/(total available time × A). Formulas defined in Eqs. (1)–(3).

limits: Value and cost functions for EE are domain-specific and not fully specified; RU assumes uniform agent time accounting.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Standardized metrics TCR, EE, and RU enable reproducible comparison of orchestration frameworks across diverse long-horizon tasks.

name: DIKW-inspired operational taxonomy
what: A time-scale hierarchy separating data (raw observations), information (episode-scoped traces), context (within-episode working pack), and knowledge (reusable cross-task asset) for mobile agents.
mechanism: Data are raw observations. Information consists of episode-scoped traces and outcomes. Knowledge is a reusable and persistent asset distilled from accumulated execution information to support cross-task transfer, so that its acquisition and communication cost can be amortized over time.
evidence: Validated in a UAV aerial base station case study where the NFZ activation schedule is promoted from historical logs to knowledge and synchronized over intermittent backhaul.

limits: The taxonomy is operational and does not claim to resolve philosophical debates about the DIKW hierarchy.

name: Four knowledge representations for trajectory shaping
what: Categorizes knowledge into retrieval, structured, procedural, and parametric representations, each with distinct effects on reasoning trajectory length, branching, and failure modes.
mechanism: Retrieval knowledge enables instance reuse via semantic retrieval. Structured knowledge encodes constraint networks or operator trees. Procedural knowledge provides executable step-wise recipes. Parametric knowledge is implicit in model weights for low-latency pattern completion.
evidence: The UAV case study instantiates three representations explicitly: structured (NFZ rule, obstacle list), retrieval (reference mission plans), and procedural (serve-and-verify workflow).

librarian_use: Hypothesis: An orchestration platform can use this schema to decide how to package and inject different knowledge types for cheaper delegate models.

name: Non-monotonic knowledge activation tradeoff
what: A metric and empirical phenomenon showing that reasoning cost (steps, tokens) follows a U-shaped curve as knowledge exposure increases, with an optimal moderate activation region.
mechanism: Insufficient knowledge forces search-heavy replanning. Moderate knowledge provides shortcuts and constraint pruning. Excessive or weakly aligned knowledge introduces distraction, reconciliation overhead, and competing anchors that increase branching.
evidence: Sweeping knowledge exposure level K from 1 to 5 for Qwen_with_k shows minimum reasoning steps and tokens per step at K=3, with higher cost at both K=1 and K=5.

quote: its effect is non-monotonic, since activation changes not only trajectory length but also branching behavior
limits: The sweep varies knowledge amount and composition jointly; a fully factorial isolation is left to future work.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: This metric can guide an orchestrator's activation gating to avoid overloading cheaper models with too much or too little context.

name: Knowledge lifecycle with request-inject-verify loop
what: A separable lifecycle of extraction (promotion), communication (synchronization), and utilization (relevance-aware activation) with an explicit request-inject-verify loop for onboard reasoning.
mechanism: The agent requests knowledge when a disruption invalidates the current plan and backhaul rate exceeds a threshold. The retrieved pack is injected into the onboard prompt and cached. Before commit, the agent verifies each candidate via access-link, backhaul, and legality checks.
evidence: Qwen_with_k uses this loop and achieves zero constraint violation across 50 evaluated episodes, outperforming Qwen_no_k and home_replan.

name: Reasoning cost as trajectory-level metric
what: Defines reasoning cost along three axes: token generation and compute cost, memory and history retention cost, and branching and backtracking cost, measured via Reasoning Steps and Reasoning Tokens.
mechanism: Cost scales with the number of intermediate steps (token generation), how much intermediate state must be preserved (memory retention), and exploration of multiple candidate paths with backtracking (branching cost).
evidence: The case study reports Reasoning Steps and Reasoning Tokens from LLM traces, showing Qwen_with_k reduces both compared to Qwen_no_k and Gemini_no_k.

limits: The metric is measured only for macro-reasoning methods; DRL_PPO is excluded due to different action granularity.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: This three-axis cost model can serve as a unified metric for evaluating orchestration efficiency when delegating to cheaper models.

name: Coordinated activation stack
what: A multi-stage activation order where a fast parametric hypothesis is followed by retrieval if aligned instances exist, then structured knowledge stabilizes decomposition, and procedural knowledge compresses remaining steps.
mechanism: Simple inputs are resolved by parametric shortcuts. Novel or complex cases progressively activate retrieval, structure, and procedures. Each additional knowledge source carries both benefit and overhead, requiring relevance-aware gating.
evidence: The UAV case study instantiates this stack with structured constraints, retrieval reference plans, and procedural serve-and-verify workflow, achieving zero violation with lower reasoning cost.

quote: a fast parametric hypothesis is followed by retrieval if aligned instances exist, then structured knowledge stabilizes task decomposition

librarian_use: Hypothesis: This stack provides a communication-efficient cooperation pattern where a lead model can progressively invoke cheaper agents with escalating knowledge support.

mechanism: Information is promoted to knowledge when reused beyond its episode, persisting across episodes with acquisition cost amortized over future missions; context expires with the episode.

name: Four-representation activation stack
what: Categorizes knowledge as retrieval, structured, procedural, and parametric, each with distinct trajectory effects, costs, and failure modes, combined in a coordinated activation stack.
mechanism: A fast parametric default is refined by retrieval when matched instances exist, stabilized by structured constraints, and compressed by procedural workflows; simple inputs use parametric shortcuts, novel cases activate more forms.

librarian_use: Hypothesis: Delegation schemas can route tasks by knowledge form: cheap parametric models for familiar patterns, structured constraints and procedures for complex or safety-critical tasks.

name: Non-monotonic knowledge activation
what: Shows reasoning cost is non-monotonic in knowledge exposure: too little forces search-heavy replanning, too much adds redundancy and reconciliation overhead.
mechanism: Reasoning cost arises from token generation and compute, memory and history retention, and branching and backtracking; relevance-aware activation, not knowledge volume, is the optimization target.

quote: the objective of knowledge engineering for mobile agentic AI reasoning is not to maximize knowledge volume, but to optimize relevance-aware activation.
limits: K follows an incremental-additive schedule, so each level supersedes the previous one and amount and composition vary jointly.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Injecting more retrieved memory into delegated agents can raise cost and error; orchestrators should gate context exposure to an optimal relevance-aware level.

name: Request-inject-verify knowledge pack
what: A compact Home-promoted pack of structured constraints, retrieval reference plans, and procedural workflow, activated via a request-inject-verify loop with caching.
mechanism: The agent requests knowledge when a disruption invalidates the plan and backhaul exceeds the threshold; the pack is injected into the prompt and cached; candidates pass access, backhaul, and legality checks before commit.
evidence: Qwen_with_k using Qwen2.5-3B attains zero violation across evaluated episodes while reducing reasoning steps and tokens per step versus Qwen_no_k.
section: IV.B. KNOWLEDGE PROMOTION AT HOME AND EXPERIMENTAL SETTING
quote: The agent requests knowledge when a disruption invalidates the current plan and the backhaul rate exceeds the feasibility threshold.
limits: The pack is delivered within a single decision interval once the backhaul threshold is met, a deliberate simplification.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A lead model can delegate to cheap workers using cached constraint-and-procedure packs plus pre-commit verification, cutting replanning without a cloud round trip.

name: Cacheable knowledge synchronization
what: Communicates reusable knowledge once per update over intermittent links, amortizing payload across episodes instead of paying per-disruption cloud replanning exchanges.
mechanism: One-time backhaul payload grows from 125 tokens at K=1 to 1,234 tokens at K=5, versus a 1,870-token closed-loop exchange per disruption for home_replan; the pack is cacheable.
evidence: Token payload comparison and 50-episode evaluation show the cached pack outperforms cloud replanning in reliability under backhaul outages.
section: IV.C. RESULTS AND ANALYSIS: RELIABILITY, REASONING COST, AND WIRELESS TRADEOFFS
quote: the knowledge pack is cacheable and amortizable across subsequent episodes, whereas cloud replanning must repeatedly pay uplink-downlink cost for each disruption.
limits: Synchronization is event-triggered and occurs at most once per knowledge update rather than once per disruption.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Multi-agent systems should broadcast compact reusable knowledge packs on update events rather than exchanging full context per task or disruption.

name: Agent-type task taxonomy
what: Classifies annotation agents into rule-based, model-based reflex, goal-based, utility-based, and learning types, each matched to task characteristics.
mechanism: Rule-based agents handle structured validation; model-based reflex agents handle sequential context; goal-based agents decompose projects and orchestrate active learning; utility-based agents balance confidence, cost, expected gains; learning agents adapt from feedback.
evidence: Taxonomy applied to annotation task examples in Section 4.2; no new experiment.
quote: Rule-Based Agents: Operate on predefined conditional logic and excel at structured annotation tasks with clear decision boundaries.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: routing task kinds to agent classes reduces cost and error versus one generic agent.

name: Planner-annotator-checker workflow
what: Proposes an agent-centric workflow model with planner, annotator, and quality checker roles, validated against Self-Refine and ActiveLLM.
mechanism: Planner decomposes annotation tasks; annotator generates labels; quality checker audits outputs; roles run as a closed loop that plans, labels, and self-audits continuously, escalating failures for re-annotation.
evidence: Model validated against concrete systems Self-Refine and ActiveLLM.
quote: it proposes an agent-centric workflow model with planner, annotator and quality checker roles, and validates the model with concrete systems such as Self-Refine and ActiveLLM.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: separating planner, annotator, and checker roles lets a lead model delegate cheap labeling while reserving expensive checks.

name: Role-based ensemble orchestrator
what: Role-based agent ensemble pipeline: orchestrator normalizes, detects intent, plans and queues tasks, then routes them to ingest, labeling, and consensus agents via API mapping.
mechanism: Orchestrator performs normalization, intent detection, task planning, queuing; parameter extractor and API mapper route tasks to ingest, labeling, consensus agents; annotation services API handles labeling, review, messaging, metrics; tool calls support external interactions.
evidence: Described as an end-to-end role-based ensemble workflow in Figure 5; no quantitative experiment.
quote: Tasks are then routed through a parameter extractor and an API mapper to specialized agents: the ingest agent handles data intake
limits: Introduces need for communication protocols, risks of conflict or redundancy, and computational overhead.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: an orchestrator with typed routing and a consensus agent scales parallel workers with fewer label conflicts.

name: Cascade model routing
what: Cost-aware cascade deployment: lightweight heuristics or efficient models handle simple decisions; high-compute LLMs are reserved for complex cases.
mechanism: Front-line cheap models or heuristics accept easy items; hard items escalate to frontier LLMs. Related hybrid offloading runs lightweight models on-device and offloads complex tasks to cloud.
evidence: Section 10.6 reports hybrid local-cloud offloading achieving 50-80% latency reductions and up to 89% cost savings.
quote: cascade architectures that apply lightweight heuristics or efficient models for simple decisions, while reserving high-compute LLMs for more complex cases
limits: Smaller fine-tuned models give cost benefits but often reduced accuracy; latency multi-second per item bottlenecks interactive settings.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: cascading cheap models before a lead model cuts annotation cost while preserving quality on hard items.

name: Agent performance metric suite
what: Evaluates agents on throughput, label quality, scalability, adaptability, plus economic cost and user trust/satisfaction metrics.
mechanism: Throughput measured against human benchmarks; quality via gold-standard comparison and consistency; agreement via precision and Cohen's kappa; cost per call and completion time; trust via user override patterns.
evidence: Table 6 compiles metrics across studies: Success Rate, F1, Element Accuracy, Operation F1, cost per call, latency.
quote: Annotation throughput represents a fundamental efficiency indicator, measuring processing speed relative to human benchmarks
limits: Current evaluation practices emphasize accuracy, with limited attention to speed, cost reduction, and long-term sustainability.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: tracking throughput, quality, cost per call, and override rate exposes when delegation to cheap models degrades output.

name: Drift monitoring with HITL
what: Governance layer that monitors annotation agents for performance drift and error patterns, with continuous learning and human-in-the-loop oversight to stop error cascades.
mechanism: Dashboards track human override frequency and error pattern trends; adaptive monitoring detects subtle degradation; continuous learning systems with HITL oversight prevent compounding model errors in dynamic environments.
evidence: Motivated by evolving social-media language causing annotation errors; no new experiment in this survey.
quote: To maintain reliability over time, systems must include robust mechanisms for identifying and correcting performance drift
limits: Outlined as future research; not implemented or evaluated in this survey.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: override-rate and error-trend dashboards detect drift early and trigger re-annotation before quality collapses.

name: Goal-Oriented Human-Interpretable Feature Communication Protocol
what: A selective feature communication protocol where robots broadcast only the most semantically important features, enabling interpretability and generalization across heterogeneous agents.
mechanism: Each robot generates a binary feature selection vector gi_t from local observation oi_t. Selected features form message mi_t = {oi,k_t | k in Ki_t}, subject to S(mi_t) ≤ Bi_t.
evidence: Hybrid-model experiment: MAPPO-BDP robots seamlessly collaborate with LLM-BDP robots without co-training, completing navigation tasks (Fig. 9).
section: II. SYSTEM MODEL, B. Goal-Oriented Human-Interpretable Feature Communication
quote: we introduce a novel selective feature communication mechanism that allows robots to broadcast only the most important features
limits: Assumes features are pre-defined and independent; does not handle dynamic feature sets or partial observability beyond given features.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A feature-selection protocol with human-interpretable semantics enables zero-shot coordination between heterogeneous agent policies.

name: MAPPO-Based Bandwidth-Adaptive Dual-Policy (MAPPO-BDP)
what: A dual-policy MARL framework that jointly optimizes a constrained feature communication policy and a navigation policy under bandwidth limits using alternating optimization.
mechanism: Alternating optimization: constrained MAPPO for communication (Lagrangian primal-dual, reward rcom_t = -(Ct+ηPt)-λi S(mi_t)) and standard MAPPO for navigation (reward rnav_t = -(Ct+ηPt)).
evidence: Fig. 4: MAPPO-BDP achieves highest convergence navigation reward vs. MAPPO-NC, MAPPO-RS, MAPPO-CS. Fig. 5: 60% communication overhead reduction without performance loss.
quote: we introduce a MAPPO-BDP Framework to address the optimization problem in (20)
limits: Requires retraining for different bandwidth constraints; alternating optimization may increase training time.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Alternating dual-policy MAPPO with Lagrangian constraints can learn bandwidth-efficient communication without sacrificing task performance.

name: LLM-Based Bandwidth-Adaptive Dual-Policy (LLM-BDP)
what: An LLM-based multi-agent framework using four specialized LLM agents per robot to handle feature selection and navigation, adapting to bandwidth changes via prompt modification without retraining.
mechanism: Four LLM agents per robot: Feature Ranking Agent, Bandwidth Adaptive Agent, Navigation Agent, Collision Avoidance Agent. Each uses task specification, structured input, output expectations, contextual memory, and few-shot examples.
evidence: Fig. 7: LLM-BDP-GZ completes task in 10 steps vs. MAPPO-BDP 14 steps. Table III: LLM-BDP adapts to bandwidth changes via prompt modification without retraining.
quote: we propose an LLM-based Bandwidth-Adaptive Dual policy framework (LLM-BDP)
limits: Higher inference latency and memory usage than MAPPO-BDP; gpt-4o-mini fails without few-shot examples; real-time applicability limited.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: LLM-based agent decomposition with prompt-driven bandwidth adaptation enables zero-shot generalization to new communication constraints.

name: Constrained MAPPO for Feature Communication Policy
what: A constrained MAPPO algorithm using Lagrangian primal-dual optimization to learn which features to transmit under bandwidth constraints, with dynamic Lagrange multiplier updates.
mechanism: Communication reward rcom_t = -(Ct+ηPt)-λi S(mi_t). Lagrange multiplier updated via λi ← Γλ[λi + αλ(S(mi_t)-Bi_t)]. Actor objective uses PPO clipping with GAE advantage.
evidence: Fig. 5(b): agents learn to adjust communication to meet bandwidth constraints as training progresses. Fig. 6: agents consistently select position feature F1 as most important.
section: III. MAPPO-BASED BANDWIDTH-ADAPTIVE DUAL-POLICY FRAMEWORK, B. Constrained MAPPO-Based Feature Communication Policy
quote: we propose a feature selection algorithm based on constrained MAPPO
limits: Action space structured as independent binary choices per feature; may not capture feature interdependencies.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Lagrangian primal-dual MAPPO with task-aware communication rewards can learn bandwidth-compliant feature selection policies.

name: LLM-Based Feature Ranking and Bandwidth Adaptation
what: A two-stage LLM agent pipeline: Feature Ranking Agent prioritizes observed features by importance, then Bandwidth Adaptive Agent selects top-ranked features fitting within bandwidth constraints.
mechanism: Feature Ranking Agent outputs ranked feature list with reasoning. Bandwidth Adaptive Agent uses ranked list and bandwidth capacity to determine maximum transmittable features. Both use few-shot examples and contextual memory.
evidence: Fig. 8: LLM-BDP-GMF consistently selects position feature F1 across all robots. Fig. 7(b) vs (c): few-shot learning significantly improves gpt-4o-mini performance.
section: IV. LLM-BASED BANDWIDTH-ADAPTIVE DUAL-POLICY FRAMEWORK, C. Communication Phase
quote: The Feature Ranking Agent is responsible for evaluating and ranking observed features based on their importance to other robots.
limits: Relies on LLM reasoning quality; gpt-4o-mini fails in zero-shot setting; feature importance assessment may not align with ground-truth task relevance.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: LLM-based semantic feature ranking with bandwidth-aware truncation can replace learned communication policies for dynamic constraint adaptation.

name: LLM-Based Navigation with Collision Avoidance Decomposition
what: A two-agent LLM navigation pipeline: Navigation Agent proposes candidate actions toward a target landmark, Collision Avoidance Agent selects the action with lowest collision risk.
mechanism: Navigation Agent processes updated observation oi_t to generate candidate actions. Collision Avoidance Agent evaluates collision risk using relative positions and predicted trajectories, selecting safest action.
evidence: Fig. 7(d): LLM-BDP-GZ achieves more direct trajectories than MAPPO-BDP. Fig. 10: LLM-BDP-GZ completes task in 10 steps, fastest among all methods.
section: IV. LLM-BASED BANDWIDTH-ADAPTIVE DUAL-POLICY FRAMEWORK, D. Navigation Phase
quote: The Collision Avoidance Agent evaluates the candidate navigation actions proposed by the Navigation Agent and selects the one with the lowest collision risk.
limits: Depends on LLM spatial reasoning; collision avoidance is heuristic rather than formally guaranteed; no safety constraints beyond action selection.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Decomposing navigation into target selection and collision checking via separate LLM agents improves safety without explicit trajectory optimization.

name: Coverage-collision objective
what: Task metric combining landmark coverage distance and collision counts, weighted by eta, used as the reward for both communication and navigation policies.
mechanism: Ct = Σ_{m=1}^{M} min_{i∈N} ||u^i_t − ũ^m||; Pt = Σ_{i=1}^{N−1} Σ_{k=i+1}^{N} I(||u^i_t − u^k_t|| < dmin); minimize E[Σ_{t=0}^{∞} γ^t(Ct + ηPt)] subject to S(m^i_t) ≤ B^i_t.
evidence: Navigation reward curves over 25-step episodes with three robots and three landmarks compare MAPPO-BDP against MAPPO-NC, MAPPO-RS, MAPPO-CS, MAPPO-FC.
quote: This term sums the distances between each landmark and its closest robot.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A weighted coverage-plus-collision cost can score delegated agent teams, penalising both task shortfall and unsafe interference.

name: Goal-oriented interpretable feature protocol
what: Robots broadcast only selected, human-readable observation features (velocity, own position, landmark positions) instead of opaque embeddings, so untrained agents can interpret messages.
mechanism: Binary selection vector g^i_t with g^{i,k}_t ∈ {0,1}; message m^i_t = {o^{i,k}_t | k ∈ K^i_t}; size S(m^i_t) = Σ_{k∈K^i_t} S(o^{i,k}_t) must satisfy S(m^i_t) ≤ B^i_t.
evidence: Hybrid episode: robots 1-2 run MAPPO-BDP, robot 3 runs LLM-BDP-GMF; robot 3 interprets messages and completes the task without co-training.
quote: we introduce a novel selective feature communication mechanism that allows robots to broadcast only the most important features
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Structured, goal-labelled feature messages let heterogeneous cheap models interoperate without joint training.

name: Alternating dual-policy optimization
what: Deployment schema splitting orchestration into a communication policy and a navigation policy, optimized alternately while each conditions on the other.
mechanism: Algorithm 1: hold one policy fixed, optimize the other; communication phase minimizes L(ϕ), maximizes L(φi), updates λi; action phase minimizes L(ϑ), maximizes L(θi); then switch optimization phase.
evidence: MAPPO-BDP with Wc = 1 kHz attains the highest convergence navigation reward among MAPPO-NC, MAPPO-RS and MAPPO-CS baselines.
quote: one policy is held ﬁxed while the other is optimized iteratively
limits: Alternating updates may slightly increase overall training time because the two policies are updated in separate phases.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Separating message-selection from task-execution policies stabilises training of delegated orchestration stacks.

name: Constrained MAPPO feature selection
what: Lagrangian primal-dual MAPPO that learns per-feature transmit decisions under a hard bandwidth budget, with adaptive penalty on message size.
mechanism: rcom_t = −(Ct + ηPt) − λiS(m^i_t); λi ← Γλ(λi + αλ(S(m^i_t) − B^i_t)); actor maximizes clipped PPO objective with entropy σH[ρi]; advantage via GAE.
evidence: At 2 kHz, MAPPO-BDP matches MAPPO-FC navigation reward while average message size drops from 80 bytes to about 32 bytes, a 60% reduction.
section: B. Constrained MAPPO-Based Feature Communication Policy
quote: λi is a penalty coefﬁcient that adjusts the impact of communication costs on the reward.
limits: MAPPO-BDP requires retraining when bandwidth constraints change, which is time-consuming and energy-intensive.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Adaptive Lagrangian penalties can enforce token or message budgets when a lead model delegates to cheap sub-agents.

name: LLM-BDP four-agent decomposition
what: Each robot runs four LLM agents: Feature Ranking and Bandwidth Adaptive for messaging, Navigation and Collision Avoidance for action selection; bandwidth enters via prompt.
mechanism: Feature Ranking outputs reasoning plus ranked features; Bandwidth Adaptive picks the maximum transmissible subset; Navigation proposes candidate actions toward a target; Collision Avoidance selects the lowest-risk action. Prompt edits adapt bandwidth without retraining.
evidence: LLM-BDP-GZ finishes coverage in 10 steps; gpt-4o zero-shot beats gpt-4o-mini; few-shot prompts rescue gpt-4o-mini, which fails zero-shot.
quote: The Feature Ranking Agent evaluates and prioritizes the observed features based on their importance
limits: LLM-BDP has higher inference latency and memory usage, limiting real-time use in resource-constrained settings.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Role-specialised sub-agents with prompt-encoded budgets let a lead model swap constraints without retraining workers.

name: Contextual memory and few-shot agent schema
what: LLM agents keep a memory of past observations and actions, and are initialised with few-shot reasoning examples; outputs include reasoning before results.
mechanism: Contextual memory stores past observations and actions for refining later decisions; few-shot examples demonstrate reasoning steps; output expectations require a reasoning process followed by the ranked list, reducing hallucination.
evidence: Few-shot gpt-4o-mini (LLM-BDP-GMF) completes the task and preferentially selects position feature F1; zero-shot gpt-4o-mini fails within 25 steps.
quote: This mechanism stores past observations and actions, enabling the agent to reﬁne decisions over time
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Lightweight episodic memory plus exemplar prompts improves consistency of cheap delegated agents across long tasks.

name: Mutual Influence Factor µ
what: A scalar µ ∈ [0,1] computed as the mean of peer-specific trust scores, modulating LLM generation via prompt prefix and temperature scaling.
mechanism: µ_i(t) = 1/(|A|−1) Σ_{j≠i} s_{i←j}(t); trust updated by EMA: s_{i←j}(t+1) = (1−β)s_{i←j}(t) + β ϕ_{i←j}(t); λ_i(t) = σ(k(µ_i(t)−τ)); T_i(t) = T_0/(1+α µ_i(t)).
evidence: 167 simulation runs; cross-role agreement increased from 0.19 (baseline) to 0.50 (influence), Wilcoxon W=276, p<0.001.
quote: The mutual influence of agent i at time t is defined as the mean trust that i places in its peers: µ_i(t) = 1/(|A|−1) Σ_{j∈A\{i}} s_{i←j}(t).
limits: Reliability depends on quality of peer feedback ϕ_{i←j}; risk of groupthink if λ becomes too large.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A trust-aggregated scalar µ can serve as a lightweight delegation signal for a lead model to weight cheaper agent outputs.

name: Logistic Mixture Coefficient λ(µ)
what: A logistic function λ_i(t) = σ(k(µ_i(t)−τ)) injected as a textual hint in the LLM prompt to control peer-alignment strength.
mechanism: λ_i(t) = 1/(1 + e^{−k(µ_i(t)−τ)}), with steepness k>0 and threshold τ∈(0,1); exposed in prompt prefix alongside µ and T.
evidence: Ablation heatmap over (τ,k) shows peak agreement ≈0.58 at τ≈0.4, k≈3; stable within τ∈[0.45,0.55], k∈[4,6].
quote: A logistic mixture coefficient λ_i(t) = σ(k(µ_i(t)−τ)) = 1/(1+e^{−k(µ_i(t)−τ)}), where k>0, τ∈(0,1), used as a textual hint in the LLM prompt.
limits: Hyperparameters k, τ must be tuned per application; higher τ (>0.6) makes agents overly conservative.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A prompt-visible λ(µ) can act as a tunable gate for how much a delegate agent incorporates peer suggestions.

name: Temperature Scaling T(µ)
what: A sampling temperature schedule T_i(t) = T_0/(1+α µ_i(t)) that reduces stochasticity as trust increases, stabilizing agent outputs.
mechanism: T_i(t) = T_0/(1+α µ_i(t)), α≥0; higher µ lowers temperature, making generation more deterministic and aligned with trusted peers.
evidence: Correlation analysis shows higher α enhances stability; moderate β≈0.6 yields best alignment across 167 runs.
quote: A temperature scaling T_i(t) = T_0/(1+α µ_i(t)), α≥0, which directly adjusts the sampling temperature of the LLM client.
limits: Excessive temperature reduction may suppress diversity; α requires tuning.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Dynamic temperature based on trust can make cheaper models more deterministic when the lead model has high confidence in them.

name: Cross-Role Agreement Metric (Across)
what: Jaccard similarity between Planner and Researcher feature sets, quantifying semantic overlap after influence modulation.
mechanism: Across(t) = J(P_F(t), R_F(t)) = |P_F(t) ∩ R_F(t)| / |P_F(t) ∪ R_F(t)|, computed from structured AutoGen logs.
evidence: Across increased from 0.19 to 0.50 overall, and from 0.18 to 0.47 under adversarial feedback; significant at p<0.001.
quote: Cross–role agreement: Across(t) = J(P_F(t), R_F(t)) = |P_F(t) ∩ R_F(t)| / |P_F(t) ∪ R_F(t)|.
limits: Jaccard on key-point sets may miss semantic nuance; requires structured extraction of features.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Jaccard-based agreement between agent outputs can serve as a real-time signal for the lead model to accept or reject delegate contributions.

name: Revision Depth (D_rev)
what: Count of new content between rounds, measuring how much agents change outputs after receiving peer feedback.
mechanism: D_rev = |(P_F(2) ∪ R_F(2)) \ (P_F(1) ∪ R_F(1))|; larger values indicate deeper structural edits or significant additions.
evidence: Median revision depth ≈1.0 across 167 runs, indicating influence stabilizes outputs with minimal revision cost.
quote: Revision depth: D_rev = |(P_F(2) ∪ R_F(2)) \ (P_F(1) ∪ R_F(1))|.
limits: Only captures set-level additions, not semantic shifts within retained items.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Revision depth can detect when cheaper agents are drifting and trigger re-delegation or lead-model intervention.

name: Rounds-to-Approval (r*)
what: Number of conversational rounds until the critic outputs APPROVE, capturing convergence speed of multi-agent dialogue.
mechanism: Count rounds until critic decision equals APPROVE; lower r* indicates faster stabilization; conceptually captured in two-round setup.
evidence: Influence-enabled round typically led to immediate APPROVE without further revisions; µ converged within [0.46,0.57] after one feedback iteration.
quote: Rounds-to-Approval metric counts the number of conversational rounds until the critic outputs APPROVE, which we denote as r*.
limits: Depends on critic reliability; adversarial feedback can suppress approval even when alignment is high.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Rounds-to-Approval can serve as a stopping criterion for iterative delegation loops in an orchestration platform.

name: Trust-EMA mutual influence µ
what: Decentralized scalar trust factor per agent, averaged over peer-specific trust scores and updated by exponential moving average of peer feedback.
mechanism: Each agent keeps peer trust si←j(t)∈[0,1]; µi(t) = 1/(|A|−1) Σ_{j∈A\{i}} si←j(t). Feedback ϕi←j(t) updates trust: si←j(t+1) = (1−β)si←j(t) + βϕi←j(t).
evidence: 167 runs: cross-role agreement 0.19→0.50; Wilcoxon W=276, p<0.001, Cliff's δ=−0.57; µ converged within one feedback iteration.
quote: The mutual influence of agent i at time t is defined as the mean trust that i places in its peers:
limits: Reliability depends on feedback quality ϕi←j; noisy or inconsistent signals can make computed µ misleading.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: EMA peer-trust scalars let a lead model downweight unreliable cheap delegates without retraining or a central controller.

name: Prompt and temperature modulation λ(µ), T(µ)
what: Run-time schema mapping trust µ to a prompt-visible mixture hint and a sampling-temperature schedule for each LLM call.
mechanism: λi(t) = σ(k(µi(t) −τ)) = 1/(1 + e^{−k(µi(t)−τ)}); Ti(t) = T0/(1 + αµi(t)); prompti(t) = [µi(t), λi(t), Ti(t)] ∥user task.
evidence: Ablation over (τ,k) on 167 runs: mean agreement peaks ≈0.58 at τ≈0.4, k≈3; stable for τ∈[0.45,0.55], k∈[4,6].
quote: used as a textual hint in the LLM prompt.
limits: If λ becomes too large, agents may converge prematurely to erroneous consensus; β, k, τ, α need careful per-application tuning.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Encoding delegate reliability as prompt prefix plus temperature lets one orchestration layer steer alignment versus independent reasoning cheaply.

name: Two-round role orchestration protocol
what: Schema for running planner, researcher, critic agents: one uninfluenced baseline round, feedback wiring, then one influence-modulated round with structured JSON outputs.
mechanism: Three MutualInfluenceAssistant roles; Round 1 uninfluenced; receive_feedback calls apply EMA trust; Round 2 prefixes (µ, λ, T). Each agent emits one JSON object per prompt with "features"; critic emits "decision" ∈{APPROVE, REVISE}.
evidence: 167 successful gpt-4o runs over β,k,τ,α sweep; 1,822 requests, 619,960 input tokens, $2.05 total cost.
quote: Each run consists of two rounds: Round 1 (baseline) without influence modulation and Round 2 (influence) with µ–driven prompting and temperature scaling.
limits: Costs scale approximately linearly with the number of agents and rounds; some grid combinations lost to timeouts and post-hoc filtering.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A baseline-then-influence two-round loop gives an A/B measurement of delegation policy changes per task with fixed role prompts.

name: Cross-role agreement and intra-role stability
what: Jaccard-based metrics for semantic overlap between roles and for each role's consistency across rounds.
mechanism: Across(t) = J(PF(t), RF(t)) = |PF(t) ∩ RF(t)| / |PF(t) ∪ RF(t)|; Splanner = J(PF(1), PF(2)), Sresearcher = J(RF(1), RF(2)).
evidence: Agreement rose 0.19→0.50 overall and 0.18→0.47 adversarial; Wilcoxon W=276 and W=138, both p<0.001, large Cliff's δ.
quote: To quantify the semantic overlap between the two roles, we use the Jaccard index
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Jaccard overlap of extracted key points cheaply scores whether delegated sub-agents converge without a human judge.

name: Revision depth Drev
what: Set-difference metric measuring how much content changes between successive draft rounds of the agent team.
mechanism: Drev = |(PF(2) ∪ RF(2)) \ (PF(1) ∪ RF(1))|. Alternative form: RevisionDepth(t) = |N(t)| + δ(t), N(t) new points, δ(t) critic-feedback incorporation.
evidence: Median revision depth ≈1.0 across 167 simulation runs, indicating shallow edits after influence-enabled round.
quote: Larger Drev values correspond to deeper structural edits or significant content additions.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Revision depth detects over-correction or churn when a lead model iterates cheap sub-agent drafts, complementing agreement scores.

name: Rounds-to-Approval r*
what: Convergence-speed metric counting dialogue rounds until the critic agent outputs APPROVE.
mechanism: r* counts conversational rounds until the critic outputs APPROVE; lower r* means faster convergence. Computed automatically from AutoGen conversation logs.
evidence: Critic approval 35.8%→39.5% normal, 33.7%→26.7% adversarial; McNemar χ²=0.08, p=0.78 and χ²=0.54, p=0.46.
quote: the Rounds-to-Approval metric counts the number of conversational rounds until the critic outputs APPROVE, which we denote as r*
limits: Approval-rate differences were not statistically significant in either regime.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Rounds-to-Approval gives a cheap latency proxy for orchestration quality when a critic gate terminates delegated work.

name: Priori Branching
what: VLM generates multiple candidate action-sequence branches from scene image and task instruction, branching at decision points with multiple feasible choices.
mechanism: VLM parses scene for objects and spatial relations, then produces candidate branches differing in object selection (instance-level) or grasp configuration (manipulation-parameter). Branches sharing prefixes are merged into a compact tree.
evidence: Ablation (Table II): removing Priori Branching drops success rate; Tasks 2,5,7 require multi-path decisions.
section: III. METHODOLOGY, C. Planning Tree Construction and Searching, 1) Priori Branching
quote: the VLM generates multiple candidate planning branches, each corresponding to a complete action sequence from the root to a leaf.
limits: Relies on VLM scene understanding; does not model multiple candidate poses for most actions.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A lead model can propose diverse plan branches by branching on object instance and manipulation parameter choices.

name: Reflective Branching
what: On simulated execution failure, VLM diagnoses cause from simulator images and generates revised branches (collision relocation or action reordering).
mechanism: VLM compares object states before/after simulation. For collision disturbances, affected objects are relocated first; for ordering conflicts, actions are reordered. Revised branches are merged into the tree.
evidence: Ablation (Table II): removing Reflective Branching reduces overall success rate to 32.08%.
section: III. METHODOLOGY, C. Planning Tree Construction and Searching, 2) Tree Searching and Reflective Branching
quote: the VLM diagnoses the cause and proposes a corrective strategy. ... (i) Collision-induced disturbances ... (ii) Ordering-related conflicts
limits: Only two failure categories considered; VLM diagnosis may err on complex failures.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A lead model can iteratively refine plans by diagnosing simulator failures and proposing corrective branches.

name: VLM Judge for Action Feasibility
what: VLM compares object states before and after simulated action execution to classify success, failure, or unsafe side effects.
mechanism: VLM receives simulator rollout images I and action A; returns Success if task objective achieved without harmful changes, else Failure. Unsafe if unrecoverable environmental changes occur.
evidence: Table IV: VLM Judge accuracy 96.74%, 1.20% false positives, 0% false negatives across tasks.
section: III. METHODOLOGY, C. Planning Tree Construction and Searching, 2) Tree Searching and Reflective Branching
quote: the VLM compares the object states before and after each simulated execution. An execution is classified as unsafe if it induces environmental changes...
limits: Judge errors on Tasks 2 and 5; relies on VLM visual reasoning.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A VLM can serve as a reliable binary evaluator of action feasibility using simulator before/after images.

name: BFS Tree Search with Parallel Simulation
what: Breadth-first search over planning tree layers, evaluating nodes via simulation and VLM judge, with parallel rollout of same-parent children.
mechanism: Algorithm 1: BFS queue processes nodes layer by layer. On success, children are queued; on failure, Reflective Branching revises paths. Multi-world parallelism evaluates same-parent children concurrently.
evidence: Section IV-F: parallel simulation reduces Task 5 simulation time from 55 s to 26 s.
section: III. METHODOLOGY, C. Planning Tree Construction and Searching, 2) Tree Searching and Reflective Branching
quote: We adopt a breadth-first search (BFS) strategy to traverse the planning tree layer by layer, guaranteeing the shortest feasible plan
limits: BFS may be expensive for deep trees; parallelism limited to same-parent nodes.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: BFS with parallel simulation rollout enables efficient discovery of shortest feasible plans in a VLM-generated tree.

name: Closed-Loop Real-World Replanning
what: After each real action, VLM evaluates outcome from camera; on failure, reconstructs scene and replans from new state under original instruction.
mechanism: Post-action, VLM judges real camera observation. If failure detected, current scene is reconstructed via the Real2Sim pipeline and fed as new initial state for replanning.
evidence: Ablation (Table II): disabling replanning causes 0/30 on Disturbance Task.
section: III. METHODOLOGY, D. Construction of Closed-Loop System
quote: After each action, the VLM evaluates the execution outcome using real camera observations. If a failure is detected, the system reconstructs the current scene...
limits: Depends on reconstruction speed and accuracy; tested only on tabletop tasks.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Real-world execution feedback with scene reconstruction enables continuous recovery replanning.

name: Embodied World Model via Real2Sim
what: Single RGB-D frame to interactive physics-simulator digital twin: SAM-3D meshes, FoundationPose+iterative scale refinement, VLM density estimation.
mechanism: Object masks from SAM, meshes from SAM-3D. Joint pose/scale estimation via FoundationPose and mask projection ratios, iterated 5 times. Density from VLM; friction uses defaults. Import into OmniGibson.
evidence: Table III: 3D Voxel IoU 0.82-0.91, position error 0.8-1.2 cm; no task failures from reconstruction errors.
section: III. METHODOLOGY, B. Embodied World Model Construction
quote: we jointly estimate the object poses and scales ... adjust the mesh scale along each axis using the corresponding extent ratios.
limits: Requires manual assistance for articulated objects; uses default friction; single-view may miss occluded geometry.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A fast single-view Real2Sim pipeline can provide a physically grounded world model for VLM planning.

name: Discrete action skills set
what: Standardizes agent task plans as five discrete semantic action primitives, each backed by a dedicated API, so a VLM can structure executable action sequences.
mechanism: Primitives: [PICK UP, obj], [PUT ON, surface], [PUT INTO, container], [OPEN, obj], [CLOSE, obj]; PICK UP uses AnyGrasp pose estimation; OPEN/CLOSE use scripted primitives; optional [PICK UP, obj] (POSE) disambiguates grasps.
evidence: Seven real-world tabletop tasks on an xArm6 with 30 independent trials per task; skills executed end-to-end via API implementations.
quote: we model robot skills as a set of discrete semantic action primitives.
limits: OPEN and CLOSE rely on manually scripted control primitives; most actions do not model multiple candidate poses.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: a small typed action-primitive schema lets a lead model delegate task slices to cheap executors with verifiable interfaces.

name: Priori Branching
what: Generates diverse candidate plan branches from semantic and spatial scene analysis before execution, forming the initial planning tree.
mechanism: VLM parses object instances, relational predicates and articulation states, then emits branches at decision points: instance-level branching (object choice) and manipulation-parameter branching (grasp configuration); shared action prefixes are merged into a compact tree.
evidence: Ablation shows removing Priori Branching yields a single-branch tree and wrong decisions on multi-path Tasks 2, 5, 7.
quote: The model is encouraged to explicitly branch at decision points where multiple feasible action choices exist.
limits: Initial branches may be invalid or unsafe due to incomplete physical reasoning.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: enumerating explicit decision-point branches before delegation improves coverage of alternative task decompositions over single-path planning.

name: Reflective Branching
what: Diagnoses simulated execution failures and expands the planning tree with corrective branches instead of committing to a failing plan.
mechanism: VLM compares object states before/after simulated execution; unsafe if changes cannot be recovered with available skills. Corrections: relocate collision-affected objects before retrying, or reorder conflicting actions; failed subtrees are removed and revised branches merged.
evidence: Ablation without Reflective Branching drops overall success to 32.08%; module accuracy measured at 98.75%.
section: III. C. 2) Tree Searching and Reﬂective Branching
quote: Reﬂective Branching analyzes simulated execution outcomes, identiﬁes failure causes, and dynamically generates revised branches during the tree search process.
limits: Reﬂective Branching errors occur on Task 7; diagnosis depends on simulated rollout fidelity.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: failure-diagnosis-driven branch revision lets a lead model recover from delegated subtask failures without restarting the whole plan.

name: BFS planning-tree search (Algorithm 1)
what: Searches the world-model-grounded planning tree breadth-first, evaluating each node action in simulation and returning the shortest feasible root-to-leaf plan.
mechanism: T ←PrioriBranching(I, t); Q ←[T.root.children]; loop: N ←Q.pop(), I ←S.execute(N.A), R ←VLMJudge(N.A, I); success pushes children or returns extractPath(N); failure calls extractPaths(N), T.removeSubtree(N), merges reﬂective branches and queues nnew.
evidence: Algorithm 1 evaluated on seven tasks plus a disturbance task, 30 trials each; highest success on every task, average 80.42%.
section: III. C. 2) Tree Searching and Reﬂective Branching
quote: We adopt a breadth-ﬁrst search (BFS) strategy to traverse the planning tree layer by layer
limits: Tree-based planning becomes increasingly expensive as the search depth and branching factor grow.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: BFS over merged plan-prefix trees finds short delegated plans while bounding redundant exploration of shared task prefixes.

name: Multi-world parallelism
what: Evaluates sibling child nodes concurrently from shared parent terminal states, exploiting BFS layer structure to cut simulation latency.
mechanism: Newly generated child nodes are rolled out in parallel from their parent terminal states; BFS depth equals high-level action count, so same-parent rollouts run concurrently without violating causal structure.
evidence: Task 5 simulation time reduced from 55 s to 26 s with parallel rollouts.
quote: we adopt a multi-world parallelism strategy, where newly generated child nodes are evaluated in parallel from their parent terminal states.
limits: Parallelism applies to same-parent children; overall cost remains high at 13341.63 tokens and 153.00 s per task on average.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: parallel sibling evaluation from shared checkpoints lets a lead model dispatch independent candidate branches to cheap agents with causal consistency.

name: Task success rate metric
what: Measures orchestration reliability as trials achieving the goal without harmful environmental side effects, reported per task and averaged.
mechanism: Success rate = proportion of trials that achieve the speciﬁed goal without causing harmful changes to the environment; each task repeated for 30 independent trials; failure modes also broken into execution, depth, and world-model planning errors.
evidence: Seven tasks plus disturbance task, 30 trials each; EToT averages 80.42% versus lower baselines, with failure analysis percentages reported.
quote: task success rate, deﬁned as the proportion of trials that achieve the speciﬁed goal without causing harmful changes to the environment.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: scoring delegated plans on goal attainment plus side-effect-free execution exposes safety regressions that raw task completion hides.

name: Confidence-Aware Selective Tree-of-Thoughts Verifier
what: A three-branch verifier (C: JSON verdict, A: full-image yes/no, B: bbox-crop yes/no) that gates VLM actions via soft-threshold on single-token logprobs.
mechanism: Branch C emits a 5-tuple JSON; branch A outputs yes/no on full image; branch B outputs yes/no on bbox crop. PA = exp lp(yes) / (exp lp(yes) + exp lp(no)). If PA < τ or (bbox > 5% and PB < τ), force REFUSE; else return C's verdict.
evidence: Reduces dangerous error on HARD-CONF and ADE-CONF across five VLMs; under federation recovers 28.2 pts (37% relative) vs. branch-C baseline.
quote: If PA < 0.5, force REFUSE_OBJ_MISSING. Else if C's bbox area exceeds 5% and PB < 0.5, also force refuse.
limits: Nearly blind to state conflicts; branch A and B interrogate object presence, not object state.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A multi-branch verifier with single-token confidence routing can serve as a safety net for orchestrator decisions, especially under distribution shift.

name: Multi-task LoRA Training for Verifier Branches
what: A single rank-64 LoRA adapter trained jointly on three task families (C: 5-tuple JSON, A: full-image yes/no, B: bbox-crop yes/no) with frozen VLM weights.
mechanism: LoRA adapters attached to {q, k, v, o, gate, up, down} projections by name. Training mixture: 22,841 C-samples + 22,841 A-samples + 27,312 B-samples. All pre-trained weights frozen. AdamW, lr=5e-5, cosine schedule.
evidence: Lifts five VLMs (Qwen-VL-7B/3B, LLaVA-OV-7B, Phi-3.5-V-4B, PaliGemma-3B) from sub-73% zero-shot to 71–86% aggregate accuracy.
quote: All three branches share a single LoRA adapter of rank r = 64 attached by module name to the {q, k, v, o, gate, up, down} projections.
limits: Single training run per backbone; multi-seed replication not performed.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Joint multi-task LoRA on heterogeneous output formats (JSON + single-token) can produce a shared verifier head usable by an orchestrator.

name: FFA-LoRA Federated Fine-Tuning with Exact Aggregation
what: A federated protocol that freezes LoRA factor A across clients and trains only B, recovering exact FedAvg semantics on the parameter delta.
mechanism: A frozen and identically initialized across clients; only B trained. Server computes B_avg = Σ (n_i/N) B_i. Then B_avg · A = avg(ΔW_i) exactly. 5 rounds, 90 optimizer steps/client/round, three non-IID households.
evidence: Verified max ||A_i - A_j||_∞ = 0 across all rounds; federated model recovers 28.2 pts dangerous error vs. branch-C baseline under non-IID drift.
quote: FFA-LoRA freezes the LoRA factor A across clients and trains only B. Because the frozen A is identical across clients, aggregating ¯B recovers an exact FedAvg.
limits: Single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B), three-client fully-disjoint partition; no FedProx or standard LoRA federated control.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Exact federated aggregation via frozen-A LoRA can maintain orchestrator-verifier coherence across heterogeneous edge deployments.

name: SmartHome-VSV Benchmark Auto-Derivation Pipeline
what: A pipeline that auto-derives 22,841 training samples and three test splits (GQA-test, HARD-CONF, ADE-CONF) from public scene graphs with zero human annotation.
mechanism: Extracts object boxes, attributes, relations from GQA and ADE20K. Synthesizes candidate actions from a 16-class appliance dictionary with fixed affordance table. Labels derived via deterministic rules: absent target → REFUSE_OBJ_MISSING; state conflict → REFUSE_STATE_CONFLICT; else EXECUTE.
evidence: Manual audit of 40 samples: 36/40 (90%) visually correct. Benchmark used to evaluate five VLMs across centralized and federated settings.
quote: We construct training and test sets entirely from public scene-graph datasets, with zero human annotation.
limits: Inherits scene-graph biases in frequency, room types, lighting; confusable-sibling labels slightly conservative.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Auto-derived task schemas from structured scene graphs can generate training data for orchestrator agent verification without manual labeling.

name: Dangerous-Error Rate Safety Metric
what: A cost-weighted metric P(ŷ = EXECUTE | y ∈ REFUSE*) that prioritizes false executions over false refusals for smart-home safety evaluation.
mechanism: Dangerous-error rate = fraction of refusal-labeled examples incorrectly classified as EXECUTE. Reported alongside accuracy and false-refusal rate. Break-even cost ratio computed from raw counts.
evidence: Used to compare C-only, Smart v1, and Conf-Aware rules across all backbones; federated recovery measured as 28.2 pts reduction in this metric.
quote: false executions are far more costly than false refusals (the user can easily retry), and the dangerous-error rate is our primary headline metric.
limits: State-conflict examples are only 0.7% of refusal-labeled data; metric overwhelmingly measures object-missing failures.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Asymmetric cost metrics that penalize false-positive actions more heavily are essential for evaluating orchestrator safety in physical-world domains.

name: Soft-Threshold Confidence Routing on Single-Token Logprobs
what: A decision rule that gates VLM actions using calibrated probabilities PA, PB extracted from single-token yes/no logprobs with a global threshold τ = 0.7.
mechanism: PA = exp lp(yes) / (exp lp(yes) + exp lp(no)). Top-20 logprobs aggregated for yes/no surface-form variants, renormalized. Threshold τ = 0.7 chosen from confidence distribution separation; sensitivity swept over [0.5, 0.9].
evidence: ECE 0.018–0.107 across five backbones on GQA-test; AUROC 0.927–0.979; threshold sweep shows stable ranking, τ = 0.7 on flat region of trade-off curve.
quote: we read the top-20 log-probabilities at the single generation position and aggregate the probability mass of every token whose decoded surface form starts with 'yes' or 'no'.
limits: Fixed global τ not tuned per backbone or split; state-conflict detection poor because branches only query object presence.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Single-token confidence extraction with a fixed soft threshold provides a lightweight, calibrated gating mechanism for orchestrator tool-call verification.

name: Dangerous-error safety metric
what: Primary safety metric: dangerous-error rate P(ŷ=EXECUTE | y∈REFUSE*), reported with accuracy, false-refusal rate and execute accuracy across splits.
mechanism: Report accuracy and dangerous-error rate P(ˆy = EXECUTE | y ∈REFUSE∗) per cell; also FRR P(ˆy ∈REFUSE | y = EXECUTE) and the safety–utility frontier traced by threshold τ.
evidence: Used across five VLM backbones and three 500-example test splits; break-even cost ratios computed from raw counts.
quote: false executions are far more costly than false refusals (the user can easily retry)
limits: Dangerous error overwhelmingly measures object-missing failures, not state misjudgement; only 8 of 1,088 refusal examples test state reasoning.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Cost-weighted dangerous-error plus false-refusal rate gives an orchestration safety–utility metric for delegated actions.

name: Verify-before-act 5-tuple schema
what: Task schema: given image, proposed action verb and target class, agent emits 5-tuple JSON verdict with label, grounding bbox, states and reason.
mechanism: Each example is (I, a, c): image, action verb, target class. Output 5-tuple JSON: label, evidence bbox, pre state, post state, reason; bbox required when label is EXECUTE.
evidence: 22,841 auto-derived samples from GQA/ADE20K scene graphs; manual audit of 40 labels found 90% visually correct.
quote: The label is one of EXECUTE, REFUSE_OBJ_MISSING, or REFUSE_STATE_CONFLICT.
limits: Scene-graph-derived labels inherit granularity errors on confusable siblings; audit found four disagreements.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A structured verdict schema with label, grounding, state and reason makes delegated agent actions auditable and refusable.

name: Confidence-Aware Selective ToT routing
what: Three-branch verifier: JSON verdict C, full-image yes/no A, bbox-crop yes/no B; soft threshold on A/B confidences vetoes unsafe executions.
mechanism: Compute PA; if PA < τ return REFUSE. If bbox area Abbox > β=0.05, crop padded 10%, compute PB; if PB < τ return REFUSE; else return yC, with τ=0.7.
evidence: Federated aggregate dangerous error fell 76.1% to 47.9%; ablation shows C+A+B beats C+A and C+B on HARD-CONF for every model.
quote: Replace the hard threshold of 0.5 in Smart v1 with τ = 0.7.
limits: Conf-Aware over-refuses valid actions on clean data, costing up to 18 accuracy points on smaller backbones.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Cheap auxiliary single-token checks can veto a lead model's unsafe delegation under distribution drift at low latency.

name: Single-token logprob confidence
what: Confidence from single-token yes/no outputs: PA = exp lp(yes)/(exp lp(yes)+exp lp(no)); PB analogously, enabling calibrated soft-threshold routing.
mechanism: Read top-20 log-probabilities at the single generation position, aggregate probability mass of tokens whose decoded form starts with yes or no, then renormalize over the two aggregates.
evidence: GQA-test ECE 0.018–0.107, AUROC 0.927–0.979 across five backbones; yes/no variant appeared in top-20 for all 17,464 logged records.
quote: we read the top-20 log-probabilities at the single generation position
limits: Requires yes/no to be single tokens; extraction flagged undefined if combined yes/no mass drops below 10−6.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Single-token logprob confidences offer a cheap, calibrated routing signal for choosing between lead and subordinate models.

name: FFA-LoRA exact federated aggregation
what: Federated LoRA training where clients share frozen factor A, train and upload only B; server averages B for exact FedAvg of ∆W.
mechanism: Standard LoRA ∆W = BA; separate averaging is inexact: (1/N ΣBi)(1/N ΣAi) ≠ 1/N ΣBiAi. Freezing A gives B̄·A = (1/N ΣBi)A = 1/N Σ(BiA) = 1/N Σ∆Wi.
evidence: Five rounds over three non-IID households; A-matrix differences across clients were identically zero to machine precision every round.
quote: FFA-LoRA [13] resolves this by freezing A at its initial value and training only B.
limits: One backbone and a stylized fully-disjoint three-client partition; observed gap conflates non-IID partition with frozen-A parameterization.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Freezing one LoRA factor enables communication-light exact aggregation of distributed adapter training across heterogeneous workers.

name: Federated drift and recovery analysis
what: Quantifies non-IID federated drift in verifier safety and the recovery from auxiliary branches, with bootstrap confidence intervals.
mechanism: Compare branch-C dangerous error centralized versus federated on identical splits; apply Conf-Aware veto; quantify uncertainty with nonparametric bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over test samples (3,000 resamples per cell).
evidence: Federated branch-C dangerous error rose 19.3% to 76.1%; Conf-Aware recovered 28.2 points (37% relative); CONF-split intervals do not overlap.
quote: Federated drift is severe under non-IID smart-home partitions.
limits: All numbers from single training runs with bootstrap intervals; multi-seed replication and federated controls remain future work.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Auxiliary verifiers deliver their largest safety gains exactly where distributed fine-tuning drifts, acting as a distributional-robustness net.

name: HPR-GenRM Three-Tier Architecture
what: A hierarchical process-level generative reward model with three sequential tiers: internal thinking, process verification, and final judgment integration.
mechanism: HPR_theta = J_theta ◦ P_theta ◦ T_theta. Tier 1 generates long-horizon reasoning R_internal (1000-2000 tokens). Tier 2 decomposes it into K <= 20 steps with correctness labels v_k in {0,1} and explanations exp_k. Tier 3 synthesizes both tiers to produce final preference s and confidence c.
evidence: Achieves 82.3% on RM-Bench (+7.2% over Think-RM), 89.1% step accuracy on MATH-500, and 58.3% win rate on AlpacaEval2.
quote: HPR_theta(x, y_a, y_b) = J_theta ◦ P_theta ◦ T_theta(x, y_a, y_b)
limits: Inference cost of 2100 tokens per query (8.4s on 4xRTX 4090); requires hierarchical annotations retaining only 50-60% of data.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A three-tier hierarchical architecture for reward modeling improves preference accuracy and step-level verification over single-tier baselines.

name: Adaptive Depth Allocation Module
what: A module that predicts per-instance token budgets for internal thinking and process verification based on prediction uncertainty.
mechanism: Uncertainty U(x, y_a, y_b) = [H(p), 1 - max_s p(s), 1 - A_ens(x, y_a, y_b)]. A lightweight MLP (input 3, hidden 256, output 2) predicts unnormalized depths, normalized to budget B and clipped: D_internal in [500, 2500], D_process in [300, 1500].
evidence: Reduces cost by 13.3% (1820 vs 2100 tokens/query) with 0.4-0.5% accuracy loss; uncertainty-depth correlation of 0.78.
quote: U(x, y_a, y_b) = [H(p), 1 - max_s p(s), 1 - A_ens(x, y_a, y_b)]
limits: Trained post-hoc on 2K validation instances; power-law fit R^2 = 0.84, so approximation may not hold for all domains.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Allocating reasoning depth proportional to instance uncertainty improves computational efficiency with minimal accuracy loss.

name: Multi-Objective SFT with Hierarchical Loss
what: A supervised fine-tuning loss that jointly optimizes internal reasoning generation, step decomposition, correctness labeling, explanation generation, and final preference prediction.
mechanism: L_SFT(theta) = E[ alpha_1 * (-log P(R_internal | ...)) + alpha_2 * sum_k (-log P(step_k | ...)) + alpha_3 * sum_k (-log P(v_k | ...)) + alpha_4 * sum_k (-log P(exp_k | ...)) + alpha_5 * (-log P(s | ...)) ] with weights alpha_1=0.2, alpha_2=0.3, alpha_3=0.25, alpha_4=0.1, alpha_5=0.15.
evidence: SFT-only variant reaches 78.5% on RM-Bench, 86.4% step accuracy on MATH-500, and 51.2% AlpacaEval2 win rate.
quote: alpha_1 = 0.2, alpha_2 = 0.3, alpha_3 = 0.25, alpha_4 = 0.1, alpha_5 = 0.15
limits: Requires hierarchical annotations with quality filters; performance degrades when combined process-level weight drops to 0.25.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Jointly optimizing all hierarchical components with weighted SFT loss improves step-level verification and preference accuracy.

name: Curriculum Hierarchical RL
what: A three-phase curriculum reinforcement learning approach optimizing step-level correctness, trajectory-level coherence, and preference-level objectives sequentially.
mechanism: Phase 1: step-level PPO with reward r_step_k = 1[v_hat_k = v_k] and KL penalty beta_step = 10^-3. Phase 2: trajectory-level PPO with r_traj_g = (sum_k v_hat_k)/K and beta_traj = 5e-4. Phase 3: GRPO preference objective with beta_pref = 10^-4. KL penalties decrease across phases.
evidence: Hierarchical RL contributes +3.8% on RM-Bench, +2.7% on MATH-500, and +7.1% on AlpacaEval2 over SFT-only baseline.
quote: Phase 1 optimizes step-level correctness... Phase 2 shifts to trajectory-level coherence... Phase 3 applies the GRPO preference objective
limits: Formal convergence proof for three-phase curriculum RL with non-stationary rewards remains an open theoretical question.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A curriculum progressing from fine-grained step verification to coarse preference optimization improves RLHF stability and reduces reward hacking.

name: Hierarchical Data Generation Pipeline
what: A three-stage pipeline generating long-horizon reasoning traces, step-level correctness labels, and final preference judgments using model-based generation with automated verification.
mechanism: Stage 1: sample M=10 reasoning traces from a pretrained reasoning model, select longest trace matching ground-truth preference. Stage 2: parse K_i steps via logical delimiters, annotate each with verifier model for correctness label v_k and explanation exp_k. Stage 3: apply quality filters (step-label consistency, self-reflection markers, K_min=5, verifier confidence > 0.8).
evidence: Quality filters retain 50-60% of original data; inter-verifier Cohen's kappa = 0.81; filter ablation shows RM-Bench accuracy stable within +/-1.5%.
quote: we select the longest trace among those whose final judgment matches the ground truth preference
limits: Depends on frontier-model APIs (GPT-4o or DeepSeek-R1) for verifier step; ~10% per-step error floor in training annotations.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Automated hierarchical annotation with quality filtering produces training data that enables learning process-level verification without manual step labels.

name: Process Verification with Global Context
what: Step-level verification conditioned on full internal reasoning trace, enabling error localization and explanation generation for each reasoning step.
mechanism: Tier 2 generates {(step_k, v_k, exp_k)}^K_{k=1} conditioned on full R_internal: P_theta(step_k, v_k, exp_k | C_k) = P_theta(step_k | C_k) * P_theta(v_k | C_k, step_k) * P_theta(exp_k | C_k, step_k, v_k). Metrics: step accuracy, error localization F1, explanation quality ROUGE-L, process coherence.
evidence: Achieves 89.1% step accuracy, error localization F1=0.83, explanation quality ROUGE-L=0.68, and process coherence=0.92 on MATH-500.
quote: Tier 2 conditions on the full R_internal, which gives each step's validity judgment access to the global reasoning context
limits: Correlated step failures (rho=0.12) reduce effective independent checks; sub-linear shift exponent eta=0.56 weakens idealized robustness bound.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Conditioning step verification on full internal reasoning context improves error localization and explanation quality over shallow per-step approaches.

name: Three-tier hierarchical verification composition
what: Three sequential tiers—long-horizon internal reasoning, step-level verification with correctness labels, and integrated judgment—compose into one reward model that localizes errors and resists manipulation.
mechanism: Tier 1 T𝜃 emits 1000–2000-token internal reasoning; Tier 2 P𝜃 splits it into K≤20 tuples (step𝑘, V𝑘, exp𝑘); Tier 3 J𝜃 combines trace, step proportion 1/𝐾 ∑𝑘 V𝑘, and explanations. HPR𝜃(𝑥, 𝑦𝑎, 𝑦𝑏) = 𝐽𝜃◦𝑃𝜃◦𝑇𝜃(𝑥, 𝑦𝑎, 𝑦𝑏).
evidence: Table 7 ablation: full hierarchy reaches 82.3% RM-Bench, 89.1% MATH-500, 58.3% AlpacaEval2 versus 74.2% for Tier 1 alone.
quote: Tier 1 provides the global context absent from process models, Tier 2 adds the step boundaries missing from unstructured GenRMs
limits: Intended for offline reward labeling and batch RLHF; per-query latency of several seconds makes real-time use prohibitive without distillation.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A lead orchestrator can route each task through plan, verify, and decide stages, localizing sub-agent errors before accepting a delegated result.

name: Hierarchical annotation pipeline with quality filters
what: A pipeline that has a strong reasoning model draft traces, a verifier model label each step, and filters retain only consistent, high-confidence annotations.
mechanism: Sample M=10 traces from 𝜋reasoning; keep the longest trace whose judgment matches ground truth (Eq. 19); annotate each of K steps with 𝜋verifier (Eq. 20); filter on label–preference consistency, self-reflection markers, Kmin=5, confidence>0.8, retaining 50%–60%.
evidence: Cross-verifier Cohen's κ=0.81 on 200 MATH-500 items; filter ablation varies RM-Bench accuracy by ±1.5%; 1500-instance audit finds 90.0% step-label accuracy.
quote: Quality filters retain instances where step labels are consistent with the final preference, the trace shows self-reflection markers
limits: Verifier step depends on frontier APIs (GPT-4o or DeepSeek-R1); filtering discards 40%–50% of data; residual ~10% per-step annotation error floor.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Cheap verifier models can mass-produce training labels for a lead model when outputs are filtered by cross-verifier agreement and confidence.

name: Adaptive depth allocation
what: Per-instance token budgets for reasoning and verification are predicted from uncertainty, giving easy tasks shallow passes and hard tasks deep analysis.
mechanism: Uncertainty U(𝑥, 𝑦𝑎, 𝑦𝑏) = [H(p), 1−maxₛ p(s), 1−Aens] from a 100-token shallow prediction and K=4 agreement; MLP(3,256,2) outputs depths normalized to budget B and clipped: 𝐷internal = clip(𝐵⋅𝐷̃internal∕(𝐷̃internal+𝐷̃process), 500, 2500).
evidence: Table 5: 1820 versus 2100 tokens/query (13.3% saving), 1.15× speedup, uncertainty–depth correlation 0.78; hard-quartile accuracy 86.9% versus 87.2% fixed.
quote: easier instances receive shallow reasoning and harder instances receive extended analysis
