evidence: Proposed solution pathway in Section 6.1 for hallucination reduction and multi-agent dependency reconciliation; no experiments.
quote: The ReAct pattern introduces an iterative loop where agents reason about tasks, act by calling tools or APIs, and then observe results before continuing
limits: Shared memory and consistent logging are essential here, ensuring that the reflective capacity of the system is not fragmented across agents.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Wrapping cheap-model calls in reason-act-observe cycles lets a lead model catch errors before committing to the next delegation step.

name: Programmatic prompt pipelines
what: Automated, role-typed prompt templates with context fillers and retrieval variables standardize inter-agent messages, preventing coordination drift in multi-agent workflows.
mechanism: Dynamic prompts are structured by task type, agent role, or user query; automated message formatting, dependency tracking, and semantic alignment keep diverse agents consistent in real time.
evidence: Proposed solution pathway in Section 6.1 addressing prompt brittleness and coordination drift; no experiments.
quote: programmatic prompting prevents coordination drift and ensures consistent reasoning across diverse agents in real time
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Schema-constrained role prompts cut token overhead and drift when a lead model fans out to many cheap parallel agents.

name: Influence Policy Language (IPL)
what: Five-field typed policy schema compiling natural-language influence directives into deployable records: targeting, theme, intensity, timing, confidence.
mechanism: π = ⟨τ, θ, ι, ω, κ ⟩; τ∈{HUBS, BRIDGES, PERIPHERY, RANDOM}, θ∈{MORAL, ECONOMIC, IDENTITY, HYBRID}, ι,κ∈[0,1], ω∈{BURST, PERIODIC}. Effective dose δ = μ(θ) · ι · κ · B(ω).
evidence: R1 decomposition attributes gains to fields: targeting +4.5 pp, dose +1.9 pp, intervention floor +1.5 pp, across 360 compile calls.
quote: We deﬁne the Inﬂuence Policy Language (IPL) as a structured record, shown in Equation 1:
limits: Theme multipliers are stipulated, not empirically calibrated; wider multiplier ranges could yield a different targeting-to-framing attribution ratio.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: a typed delegation record with named, independently tunable fields makes orchestration decisions auditable and attributable to individual design choices.

name: Solver–critic compiler with safe fallback
what: Two-stage pipeline mapping population state snapshots to validated policies: a solver proposes, a critic risk-scores, an aggregator attenuates.
mechanism: Solver gets st = ⟨t, ¯pt, σp,t, ¯et, emax t, Ge(t), ¯crecent⟩. Reject: ι←clip(ιs/2,0.1,0.8), κ←0.7κs; HIGH: ι←clip(0.7ιs,0.1,0.9); MEDIUM: ι←clip(ιadj,0.1,1.0); LOW: unchanged. Unparseable output falls back to ⟨RANDOM, ECONOMIC, 0.5, PERIODIC, 0.65⟩.
evidence: 360 production calls: 100% parseable, zero fallbacks; adversarial stress: 20/20 risky policies flagged HIGH and rejected, moderate baseline passed 5/5.
quote: If either stage produces unparseable output, the system falls back to a safe default policy:
limits: Critic gating is verified responsive on adversarial inputs but is not exercised by the solver in production.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: a solver–critic gate with conservative attenuation and deterministic fallback reduces risky delegations while preserving orchestration throughput.

name: Degree-based targeting substitute
what: Cheap O(n) degree-based agent selection replaces O(nm) betweenness computation when choosing which parallel agents receive work or exposure.
mechanism: Select k = ⌊0.12 × n⌋ targets by highest degree (HUBS) or highest betweenness (BRIDGES); in BA graphs both sets coincide, so degree-based selection suffices.
evidence: HUBS and BRIDGES numerically identical at every timestep in BA; exposure redistribution ratio 1.5× under hubs versus 3.8× under periphery.
quote: lightweight degree-based targeting (O(n)) can replace expensive betweenness computation (O(nm)) without performance loss, a practical advantage at scale.
limits: Hub–bridge equivalence is BA-specific; it breaks in modular SBM where bridges have moderate degree.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: degree-ranked routing yields betweenness-quality delegation at lower cost on scale-free agent topologies.

name: Fatigue–diffusion–backlash exposure model
what: Exposure state with decay, one-way neighbor diffusion, capping and backlash prevents unbounded accumulation and models long-horizon habituation and reactance.
mechanism: ˜eo(t) = (1 −λ) eo(t); eo(t + 1) = ˜eo(t) + α · max(0, 1/|No| Σz∈No ez(t) − eo(t)); clip to emax; bo(t) = ρ · max(0, eo(t) −eβ).
evidence: R5 burst test: sequential dosing stays under eβ = 3.5, giving 3.27× less cumulative backlash than a 3× multiplier at equal final cooperation.
quote: The exposure update comprises three stages applied at every timestep:
limits: Agents are numerical entities with known logistic responses, not LLMs; real agents may ignore instructions or resist influence.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: decay, one-way diffusion and dose caps stabilize long-running delegated workloads against overload, saturation and agent pushback.

name: Orchestration outcome metric suite
what: Common per-timestep metrics for effectiveness, stability, equity and cost of deployed policies.
mechanism: Final cooperation ¯cﬁnal over t ∈[86, 100]; σc; cmax; polarization Var[p(C)]; exposure Gini; diffusion speed = first timestep average exposure reaches 80% of maximum; average backlash; maximum exposure.
evidence: Applied across more than 200 runs in nine experiment blocks, four topologies, four network sizes and five LLM backbones.
quote: Diﬀusion speed: the ﬁrst timestep at which average exposure reaches 80% of its global maximum, measuring how quickly inﬂuence saturates the network.
limits: Cooperation rate captures one dimension of collective behavior; polarization omits ideological clustering, and Gini omits whether the right agents receive influence.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: pairing outcome, equity and diffusion-speed metrics detects delegation policies that look effective while overloading a few subordinates.

name: Re-resolvable abstract targets under drift
what: Policies name target roles as tokens resolved against current topology at each redeployment, so retargeting survives structural change.
mechanism: At every Δt = 10, build state snapshot, compile policy, resolve token HUBS on the current graph, deploy dose δ to k targets; a frozen node list cannot retarget.
evidence: R8b graph rewire, 8 seeds: recovery and late gaps +0.005/+0.006, paired Wilcoxon p = 0.004, paired Cohen's d = 2.27 late.
quote: The advantage comes from the architectural property that HUBS is a re-resolvable abstract token rather than a frozen node list.
limits: The advantage is small (+0.6 pp); no policy parameters changed, only target resolution, and parametric shock showed no gain.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: role-token delegation re-resolved at each dispatch keeps parallel teams aligned after membership or topology churn.

name: JNSRA two-LLM orchestration
what: Two cooperating LLMs jointly optimize intent-driven slice configurations and per-BS bandwidth allocation in large multi-BS networks.
mechanism: Intent LLM maps natural-language intents to formatted slice configurations as; Agent LLM maps slice and network states to bandwidth allocation aB. Both are jointly optimized via an MDP-based framework.
evidence: Simulation on 2km x 2km Urban Macro multi-cell with four slices; JNSRA beats c-DDPG and Average, Weighted, Random heuristics on reward, satisfaction ratio, throughput.
quote: we propose the multi-LLM cooperation-based JNSRA to jointly optimize the intent-driven network slicing and resource allocation.
limits: Simulation-based setup; certain practical factors may not be fully captured.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: a lead model emitting structured configs plus a cheaper allocation agent can outperform single-model DRL on combinatorial tasks.

name: Intent LLM SFT formatting
what: Supervised fine-tuning of a small intent model to translate user intents into directly extractable structured slice configurations.
mechanism: Teacher DeepSeek-R1 produces formatted prompts and responses for training data. SFT loss LSFT = −1/L Σ_{t=1}^{L} log P(yt | p, y<t, θ) maximizes probability of the formatted response, yielding extractable as.
evidence: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B Intent LLM generates slice configurations used in joint-optimization simulation (Fig. 4b).
quote: we first pre-train Intent LLM in a Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) manner.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: teacher-generated format-constrained SFT lets a cheap model emit schemas a lead orchestrator can parse without repair.

name: Cross-attention Agent LLM with DPO
what: A Llama-based agent with cross-attention fuses slice and network modalities to output joint bandwidth allocation, trained by preference optimization.
mechanism: Slice state as ∈ R^{M×3} and network state sn ∈ R^{K×5} pass through separate Llama-based models; hidden states feed cross-attention to obtain aB. Rewards split into accept Da and reject Dr; DPO loss LDPO updates the model.
evidence: Outperforms centralized DDPG with transformer and three heuristics on reward, QoS satisfaction ratio, throughput (Fig. 4a).
quote: Agent LLM takes slice information and network status as input state, and outputs the bandwidth resource allocation for all BS.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: cross-attention over heterogeneous state modalities plus DPO gives cheap agents robust joint allocation without critic value estimation.

name: Normalized environment reward
what: Bounded reward combining per-slice satisfaction ratio with normalized delay and reserved-bandwidth intent objectives.
mechanism: renv = Σ_{m∈M} NmRm[ωd,m (max(dm)−dm)/(max(dm)−min(dm)) + ωB,m (Bmin_m − min(B̂min_m))/(max(B̂min_m) − min(B̂min_m))], each normalized term limited from 0 to 1.
evidence: Reward used to train Agent LLM via DPO and reported as total reward in Fig. 4a and 4b comparisons.
quote: which can mitigate the reward hacking issue of RLHF.
limits: Normalized terms are limited from 0 to 1 to mitigate reward hacking.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: min-max normalizing heterogeneous objective terms to [0,1] yields stable delegation rewards resistant to reward hacking.

name: Multi-LLM MDP joint training
what: Formalizes lead intent model and downstream agent as a two-step MDP so the lead learns from downstream environment outcomes.
mechanism: Initial state (sn,p); Intent LLM emits as; state becomes {as,sn}; Agent LLM emits aB, reward renv. Q(sn,p,as) = E[r(sn,p,as) + γ max_{aB} Q(sn,as,aB)] = r(sn,p,as) + γ max_{aB} r(sn,as,aB); final reward rf + γ max_{aB} renv.
evidence: Joint training improves total reward versus training the two LLMs separately (Fig. 4b).
quote: we formulate the relationship between Intent LLM and Agent LLM as an MDP.
limits: Positive samples with rf = 1 greatly outnumber negative samples rf = 0 after pre-training.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: propagating downstream agent reward back to a lead model via a Bellman-style two-step credit improves delegation decisions.

name: Orchestration evaluation metrics
what: Evaluation suite of total reward, QoS satisfaction ratio, and average throughput against DRL and heuristic baselines.
mechanism: Compare JNSRA against centralized DDPG (transformer critic) and Average, Weighted, Random allocation heuristics; report total reward, QoS satisfy ratio, average throughput in Mbps over the multi-cell simulation.
evidence: Fig. 4a, 4b show JNSRA gains on all three metrics; joint optimization especially improves total reward.
quote: JNSRA illustrates significantly better performance in terms of reward, satisfaction ratio and network throughput.
limits: Simulation-based setup; certain practical factors may not be fully captured.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: reward, task-satisfaction ratio, and throughput together measure whether cheap-model delegation preserves quality while cutting cost.

name: AgentAI lifecycle schema
what: Lifecycle schema for autonomous agents: creation by model developer, system developer, and user, then deployment, migration, human-in-the-loop oversight, and controlled shutdown.
mechanism: Deployment uses cloud-native platforms, containers, and orchestration for dynamic scheduling; migration adapts agents via fine-tuning or re-training; service discovery locates services by availability, proximity, or load; shutdown must be accepted even mid-task.
evidence: Survey synthesis of 66 articles; Fig. 4 depicts lifecycle phases and Table 3 compares domains.
quote: Once the initial creation of the AgentAI is completed, its deployment requires sophisticated infrastructures capable of supporting distributed, low-latency, and scalable execution.
limits: Real-world implementation is far from uniform; domain constraints include legal compliance, real-time responsiveness, and physical integration.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A lifecycle schema with explicit migration and shutdown hooks could structure orchestration platforms that delegate across heterogeneous models and agents.

name: Domain lifecycle attribute matrix
what: Comparative matrix mapping fine-tuning, migration, and interruptibility requirements across nine Industry 4.0 domains.
mechanism: Table 3 lists per-domain values: transportation uses edge-to-cloud dynamic deployment; networking uses service discovery and topology-driven relocation; governance mandates interruptibility for legal compliance.
evidence: Table 3 compiles lifecycle attributes for nine domains from the reviewed literature.
quote: Table 3 provides a comparative overview of key lifecycle attributes across the domains outlined in the taxonomy.
limits: Attributes are qualitative comparisons drawn from literature, not measured benchmarks.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Per-domain lifecycle attributes could guide task-to-agent routing policies that vary migration and interruption rules by workload criticality.

name: Perception-cognition-action modules
what: Component schema clustering agent internals into perception, cognition, and action modules for multimodal interpretation, reasoning, and execution.
mechanism: Perception integrates images and text via VLMs/LLMs; cognition applies RL and explicit/implicit knowledge bases for reasoning; action converts decisions into real or virtual actions refined by rewards and penalties.
evidence: Fig. 3 and Section 3.1 organize surveyed agent systems into three modules.
quote: The main components of AgentAI, as shown in Fig. 3, could be clustered in perception module, cognition module and action module.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Separating perception, cognition, and action interfaces could let a lead model delegate only the cognition step to cheaper models.

name: Agent paradigm selection table
what: Comparative table matching agent paradigms to task types using interpretability, scalability, and adaptability criteria.
mechanism: Covers symbolic reasoning agents, graph-based policies, behaviour tree agents, probabilistic/Bayesian agents, and transformer LLMs, each mapped to suitable tasks such as logistics, multi-step planning, or real-time control.
evidence: Table 2 synthesizes paradigm strengths from cited systems across four criteria.
quote: Table 2 provides a comparative overview of the paradigms discussed above along four criteria: interpretability, scalability, adaptability, and their most suitable tasks.
limits: Transformer-based LLMs currently dominate; alternatives matter where interpretability or structured reasoning is required.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Paradigm-to-task mappings could serve as routing rules for assigning subtasks to cheap symbolic, graph, or LLM workers.

name: Data flywheel feedback loop
what: Continuous refinement loop where action feedback and model customization adapt the agent to tasks and environments over time.
mechanism: Agent receives user input, retrieves structured or semantic data, reasons via LLM, executes actions, then feeds outcomes back to refine the system and customize the model.
evidence: Fig. 2 workflow diagram; no quantitative evaluation reported.
quote: The data ﬂywheel captures feedback from these actions to continuously reﬁne the system, while model customization ensures the AI adapts to speciﬁc tasks and environments
limits: Retraining becomes mandatory for new domains, edge cases, or improved accuracy.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: A feedback flywheel could detect delegation drift and trigger reassignment or fine-tuning of sub-agents in long-running orchestration.

name: Decentralized multi-agent coordination blueprint
what: Future coordination design for networks of edge agents using decentralized negotiation, collaborative planning, and distributed consensus.
mechanism: Supply-chain agents representing suppliers, manufacturers, and logistics providers negotiate contracts, reschedule production, and reroute deliveries after disruptions; local agents rebalance workloads without centralized oversight.
evidence: Section 6.3 blueprint with supply-chain and smart-manufacturing scenarios; no experiments.
section: 6.3. Toward a blueprint for agentAI in industry 6.0
quote: These agents must collaborate in real time through decentralized negotiation, collaborative planning, and distributed consensus protocols.
limits: Vision requiring interdisciplinary research in graph-based communication, explainable MARL, and intent-aware planning; not yet implemented.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: Decentralized negotiation and consensus protocols could coordinate parallel cheap agents with less lead-model communication overhead.

name: Sliced Shapley Value (SSV) head importance
what: Scores each cooperating unit's contribution to global utility by averaging complementary contributions over a few sampled coalition sizes instead of all coalitions.
mechanism: Treats each head/group as a player. SSV L 𝑖= 1 |L| 𝑛 ∑︁ 𝑗=1 SV𝑖,𝑗· I L 𝑗, where SV𝑖,𝑗 averages U(S) − U(H \ S); error bounded by O(√(1/|L|)).
evidence: LongBench masking tests: removing CoKV's top-ranked groups drops Qwen3-32B to 13.68% average versus 33.91% for HeadKV-R2 (Table 2, page 9).
quote: The sliced Shapley value of head ℎ𝑖with respect to L is defined as the expected complementary contribution over 𝑗-coalitions for 𝑗∈L:
limits: Approximation to exact Shapley value; error bounded by O(√(1/|L|)) assuming SV𝑖,𝑗∈[𝑎,𝑏].
librarian_use: Hypothesis: SSV-style coalition sampling can rank delegated sub-agents by cooperative contribution, replacing isolated per-agent scoring in orchestration budget allocation.

name: Monte Carlo complementary-contribution estimation
what: Efficient algorithm estimating all units' importance jointly: one masked/unmasked evaluation updates every member of the sampled coalition, cutting redundant evaluations.
mechanism: For k=1..M sample permutation 𝜋𝑘, pick 𝑗∈L, set S={𝜋𝑘[1],…,𝜋𝑘[𝑗]}, compute 𝑢=U(S)−U(H\S), add 𝑢 to each 𝑖∈S; average SV𝑖,𝑗/𝑚𝑖,𝑗. Complexity O(𝑇|L|ln(2|L|/𝛿)/𝜖²).
evidence: Theorem 2 proves (𝜖,𝛿)-approximation with time O(𝑇|L|ln(2|L|/𝛿)/𝜖²) versus O(𝑇𝑛ln(2𝑛/𝛿)/𝜖²) for standard Shapley approximation.
quote: we adopt a Monte Carlo approach that iteratively estimates the expected complementary contribution of each (𝑖, 𝑗)-coalition
limits: Each complementary-contribution evaluation costs one validation-dataset inference; estimate quality depends on sample count M.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: shared complementary-contribution updates let a lead model score many cheap parallel agents with far fewer joint evaluation runs.

name: Cooperation-aware cache budget allocation
what: Distributes a shared memory budget across units proportionally to normalized importance scores, zeroing the least useful units and reserving a fixed local window.
mechanism: NSV L 𝑖= SSV L 𝑖−min𝛼(SSV L) / max(SSV L)−min𝛼(SSV L); then 𝑐𝑖= 𝐵· NSV L 𝑖 ∑︁𝑛 𝑗=1 NSV L 𝑗 + 𝑠, with α least-important heads set to 0.
evidence: LongBench: Llama3-8B keeps 96.13% of full-KV performance with 128 KV pairs per cache, about 1.6% of full cache (page 8).
quote: the cache size 𝑐𝑖allocated to head ℎ𝑖is determined by the local window size 𝑠and linearly distributing the remaining shared cache size 𝐵
limits: Requires hyperparameter α, the sole allocation hyperparameter, selected by grid search on a validation set.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: proportional-to-importance budget splitting with a floor reserve can allocate context or memory across delegated agents under a hard global budget.

name: Local-window-guided token eviction
what: Per-unit eviction algorithm retaining top-scoring tokens outside a recent local window, where scores come from pooled attention of window queries to prefix keys.
mechanism: A𝑖= Softmax(Q𝑤𝑖𝑛 𝑖 K⊤ 𝑖); A𝑖= A𝑖.𝑚𝑎𝑥𝑝𝑜𝑜𝑙𝑖𝑛𝑔(𝑑𝑖𝑚= 1).𝑚𝑒𝑎𝑛(𝑑𝑖𝑚= 0); keep top 𝑐𝑖 outside-window KV pairs by indices, then Cat with local-window KV.
evidence: Compared under identical cache budgets with GQA and FlashAttention on LongBench, NIAH, RULER, GSM8K, MATH (Sections 6.1-6.2).
quote: Attention scores from these local windows to the remaining tokens are aggregated via pooling, with higher-scoring tokens retained in the cache for each head.
limits: Eviction runs after the prefilling phase of each layer; local window size set to s = 8.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: recency-window plus pooled-usage scoring gives a deterministic memory policy for trimming long agent transcripts while preserving retrieval-critical spans.

name: Offline precomputed shared importance deployment
what: Deployment schema: precompute importance scores once on generic validation data, ship them with model weights, and reuse them at inference without re-estimation.
mechanism: Precompute per-unit SSV offline on generic validation sets, distribute scores alongside weights; at inference map scores directly to eviction budgets or quantization bit-widths, with no per-request computation.
evidence: Averaged LongBench scores transfer to GSM8K, MATH, NIAH and RULER without per-request re-estimation (Sections 6.2, 6.5).
quote: CoKV eliminates cold start costs through a “one-time computation, shared usage" paradigm, allowing model providers to precompute importance scores offline on generic validation sets
limits: Importance scores must be precomputed offline on generic validation sets and distributed with the model.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: precomputed, shipped routing profiles let an orchestration platform deploy delegation policies instantly with zero cold-start scoring cost.

name: SSV stability under decoding drift
what: Measures whether precomputed importance rankings stay stable across decoding steps and tasks, enabling task-agnostic reuse without per-request re-estimation.
mechanism: Compute step-wise SSV under reference-continuation teacher forcing at steps {1, 5, 10, 20, 40}; measure adjacent-step Spearman correlation and Top-100 overlap; average SSV across tasks for reusable scores.
evidence: Teacher-forced step-wise SSV on Qwen3-32B: adjacent-step Spearman 0.67-0.90, Top-100 overlap above 55%; transfer validated on GSM8K, MATH, NIAH, RULER (Section 6.5).
quote: adjacent-step Spearman correlations range from 0.67–0.90, and Top-100 overlap exceeds 55% as shown in Fig. 14
limits: Task-specific deviations exist; detailed stability analysis is deferred to the appendix.
librarian_use: Hypothesis: rank-stability checks across rollout steps can detect delegation-policy drift and trigger cheap re-scoring only when rankings degrade.

name: SIC three-stage architecture
what: Sense-Infer-Control architecture mapping process instrumentation, agentified modeling, and agentic control into one deployable schema for industrial monitoring and decision loops.
mechanism: Three stages: (1) process and instrumentation workflow maps process task, variables and QIVs into a knowledge base of mechanistic models, parametric data, solvers, physical and soft sensors; (2) agentified modeling fuses mechanistic models with AI agents; (3) SCADA/PLC control gains agency for real-time decisions.
evidence: Four case studies (motorsport, sugar crystallization, cosmetics, biomanufacturing) map Stages 1-3 onto real operations in Table 1, page 5.
section: Systematic architecture for industrial Agentic AI and generative modeling
quote: This approach consists of three key stages: (1) creating a process and instrumentation workflow to identify critical QIVs for measurement and monitoring
limits: real-time, agentic decision-making at scale demands significant computational resources and robust edge-to-cloud infrastructure
librarian_use: Hypothesis: a lead-model orchestration layer can adopt the three-stage schema to assign sensing, inference, and actuation roles to specialized cheap agents.

name: Edge-cloud hybrid agent deployment
what: Deployment schema splitting compute between trackside edge GPUs for low-latency inference and cloud training, with periodic model synchronization.
mechanism: Transportable edge GPU unit ingests telemetry for immediate inference; cloud trains generative models on historical and synthetic data, periodically synchronized to edge; generative models synthesize 'virtual sensor' streams where measurements are missing.
evidence: Zapata AI Andretti race system described in Case 1, with edge-to-cloud architecture and virtual sensor inference (pages 4-5).
section: Case 1: A motivating example of generative modeling as a soft sensor in motor sports
quote: The hybrid approach leverages the cloud for computationally intensive tasks while maintaining low-latency decision support at the edge
limits: synchronizing cloud-based model training with trackside edge deployments is crucial for providing up-to-date predictive analytics, yet remains challenging due to high data volumes
librarian_use: Hypothesis: routing latency-critical subtasks to edge or cheap local models and heavy training to a central service reduces orchestration cost without losing accuracy.

name: Group prediction ensemble aggregation
what: Parallel per-instance model ensembles whose outputs are aggregated by a group prediction model for track-wide decisions.
mechanism: For Yellow Flag and Lap Time prediction, two or more models run per car; their outputs feed a group prediction model combining signals across cars; ensembles cover lap time, yellow flag, tire degradation, race strategy.
evidence: Motorsport deployment runs ensembles built from 10+ years telemetry and simulator data, with per-car model groups feeding group prediction (page 6).
section: Case 1: A motivating example of generative modeling as a soft sensor in motor sports
quote: two or more models are used for each of the cars on the track, and those models feed a group prediction model
librarian_use: Hypothesis: a lead model can aggregate outputs from parallel cheap sub-agents via a group predictor, improving robustness over any single agent.

name: Concurrent inference throughput metric
what: Reported operational metric quantifying message throughput and concurrent model load for an agent inference fleet.
mechanism: Each model performing inference processes up to 200 messages per millisecond; close to one hundred models may run inference simultaneously during a race.
evidence: Case 1 reports near one hundred concurrent inference models and per-model message rate during races (pages 6-7).
section: Case 1: A motivating example of generative modeling as a soft sensor in motor sports
quote: Each model performing inference is capable of processing up to 200 messages per millisecond
limits: Internet connectivity at some tracks is often unpredictable in terms of reliability and latency
librarian_use: Hypothesis: messages-per-millisecond and concurrent-model count are usable benchmark metrics for sizing delegated-agent fleets under latency constraints.

name: Hybrid mechanistic-AI soft sensor
what: Schema for inferring hard-to-measure quality variables from cheap sensor inputs using mechanistic knowledge fused with machine learning.
mechanism: Easily measurable variables such as temperature and pressure feed a hybrid model combining process control expertise with machine learning to predict the Brix index in real time; outputs integrate into SCADA/DCS control.
evidence: Sugar-beet crystallization study predicted Brix index and reduced batch residence time, energy use and CO2 emissions (page 8).
quote: By leveraging easily measurable variables, such as temperature and pressure, the model successfully generated the Brix index for real-time process monitoring
limits: inconsistent sampling rates, sensor drift, and noisy measurements require data normalization and deep learning techniques to capture key time-series patterns
librarian_use: Hypothesis: cheap proxy-sensor agents plus a hybrid inference agent can substitute for expensive measurements, letting a lead model delegate estimation subtasks.

name: Qψ-TUBE hybrid quantum-classical pipeline
what: Two-module pipeline partitioning biomanufacturing scale-up tasks between microscale calibration agents and macroscale estimation agents, mixing quantum and classical solvers.
mechanism: MicroTUBE uses imaging, spectroscopy and generative models seeded with O2, CO2, pH, temperature; MacroTUBE models tracer profiles and compressed-sensing states; quantum SDP/QUBO and classical solvers split subproblems; modules integrate into Qψ-TUBE for monitoring and counterfactual simulations.
evidence: Proposed biomanufacturing scale-up architecture combining MicroTUBE and MacroTUBE with quantum and classical AI components (pages 11-12).
section: Case 4: Biomanufacturing process scale-up with quantum and classical agents
quote: Qψ-TUBE combines two modules, MicroTUBE for microscale calibration and MacroTUBE for macroscale estimation and optimization, each with experimental and computational parts
limits: However, quantum algorithms often have high computational and hardware requirements
librarian_use: Hypothesis: a lead model can partition subproblems across heterogeneous solvers by cost and capability, mirroring MicroTUBE/MacroTUBE task decomposition.
